summary.title: HTTPWTF
summary.one_liner: A tour of HTTP's odd corners: misleading Cache-Control combinations, trailers, 1XX interim status codes, the misspelled Referer header, the magic UUID in WebSocket handshakes, CORS gaps for WebSockets, and the pitfalls of X- prefixed headers.
takeaways: Cache-Control: no-cache allows storing but requires revalidation; use no-store to prevent caching of sensitive data.
HTTP trailers let servers send metadata after the body, but need TE: trailers and a Trailer header, and HTTP/1.1 needs chunked encoding.
1XX codes (100, 101, 102, 103) are interim responses for continuing, protocol switching, processing, and early link hints.
WebSockets ignore CORS, so servers must check the Origin header and/or use CSRF tokens.
Avoid X- prefixed custom headers that may later become standard; pick unique names instead.
summary.summary: The author walks through a set of HTTP features and quirks, explaining each with examples and short caveats. Topics include how Cache-Control no-cache, private, and no-store actually behave, HTTP trailers, the 1XX interim status codes (100, 101, 102, 103), the misspelled Referer header, the Sec-WebSocket-Accept handshake, WebSockets bypassing CORS, and the X- header convention. It is an opinionated, example-driven explainer rather than a formal spec, and it points to RFCs and related articles for further reading.
